questions.q: In Mulvey's account of classic Hollywood, who is the 'bearer of the look'?
choices: The male protagonist, with whom the audience is invited to identify
questions.explain: The camera, male characters and audience look at the woman while identifying with the man who drives the plot.

questions.q: A screenwriter notices the heroine only appears in close-ups as men watch her, and never gets a point-of-view shot of her own. Which idea names the problem?
questions.explain: Mulvey's analysis is about who looks and who is looked at in the grammar of shots.

questions.q: What, according to Adichie, is the real problem with stereotypes?
choices: They're incomplete, making one story the only story
questions.explain: Her point is incompleteness, not untruth.

questions.q: A reporter covers a neighborhood only through crime stories, year after year. Which warning applies most directly?
choices: The danger of a single story
Something mechanical encrusted on the living
questions.explain: Repeated single stories make one aspect stand for the whole.

questions.q: Whom does Alison Bechdel credit for the idea behind the test named after her?
questions.explain: She prefers the name Bechdel-Wallace test, and has suggested Wallace drew on Woolf.

questions.q: A film passes the Bechdel test. What can you conclude?
choices: Its women are fully realized characters
It has at least two women who talk to each other about something besides a man
It was directed by a woman
questions.explain: The test measures presence, not quality.

questions.q: Why does Thomas King set a Native creation story beside Genesis?
choices: To prove one is historically true
To show how the stories a culture tells shape what it takes as natural
To argue that only oral stories matter
questions.explain: A solitary creator and a fall versus cooperation and a shared world imply different values.

questions.q: What was bell hooks's main objection to Mulvey's 1975 essay?
choices: It ignored race, and Black women spectators who looked critically
It was too optimistic about Hollywood
It relied too little on psychoanalysis
questions.explain: hooks's 'oppositional gaze' describes resistant looking that Mulvey's model missed.

ideas: Which approach argues that classic cinema positions women as spectacle to be looked at while the man who looks drives the story?
Which approach warns that the trouble with stereotypes isn't that they're false but that they're incomplete?
Which approach treats hearing a story as making you responsible for it?
Which approach asks whether a film has two women who talk to each other about something other than a man?
